'''''Entada gigas''''', commonly known as the '''monkey-ladder''', '''sea bean''', '''cœur de la mer ''' or '''sea heart''', is a species of [[Flowering plant|flowering]] [[liana]] in the [[pea]] family, [[Fabaceae]], subfamily [[Mimosoideae]]. It is native to [[Central America]], the [[Caribbean]], northern [[South America]], and [[Africa]].<ref name="POWO"/> It is notable for having the largest [[Legume|seedpods]] in the Fabaceae.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ul30UwirsSEC |title=Amazing Plants |first=Ilil |last=Arbel |publisher=Courier Dover Publications |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-486-43336-3 |page=27}}</ref>

==Description==

===General characteristics===
[[File:Entada Wa-wa.jpg|thumb|right|''Entada gigas'' fruit]]
The fruit measures {{convert|12|cm|in|abbr=on}} across and can reach {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} long, with reports of pods up to {{cvt|2.5|m|ft|0}} long.<ref>{{ cite book |editor-last= Bailey | editor-first= Liberty Hyde | date= 1935 | title= Cyclopedia of Horticulture | location= New York | publisher= MacMillan and Co. | page= Vol. 1 p. 1116 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last= Dodge | first= Charles R. | date= 1897 | title= A Descriptive Catalogue of Useful Fiber Plants of the World | journal= U.S.D.A. Fiber Investigation Report |volume= 9 | issue= 1 | page= 157}}</ref> This pod, like all [[legumes]], is a single [[carpel]], the largest carpel of any known plant. Inside each pod are ten to fifteen [[seed]]s, each of which have a diameter of {{convert|6|cm|in|abbr=on}} and a thickness of {{convert|2|cm|in|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ekfhub2YU5EC |title=A Field Guide to Southeastern and Caribbean Seashores: Cape Hatteras to the Gulf Coast, Florida, and the Caribbean |first=Eugene H. |last=Kaplan |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |year=1988 |isbn=978-0-395-97516-9 |page=148}}</ref>  The seeds contain a hollow cavity, which gives them [[buoyancy]]. After being washed by rain into rivers and then the ocean, the seeds can [[Drift seed|drift]] long distances on [[ocean current]]s. Seed buoyancy and vitality lasts at least two years.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Yorr0tXFx2IC |title=Seeds: the Definitive Guide to Growing, History, and Lore |first=H. Peter |last=Loewer |publisher=Timber Press |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-88192-682-8 |page=66}}</ref>

==Use==
In Gabon it is used to make ropes and nets.<ref name = "Fibres">[https://books.google.com/books?id=AspmAgAAQBAJ&dq=Entada%20gigas&pg=PA153 Fibres.] p.153. (2012). Niederlande: Prota Foundation.</ref>
